From Coromandel on the 31st of October 1720

To the Most Esteemed Lord Henric Swaarde Croon, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies,

Lord and Esteemed Lords,

In continuation of our humble letter of the 9th of September last, which was sent to Your High Excellency regarding Masulipatnam [Masulipatnam], of which the copy is herewith annexed, we shall now supply as briefly as possible what was still lacking in the previous regarding the gifts made, speaking of carpentry and repairs, and also the weights that have fallen short on the merchandise, etc., at this Coast during the course of the account year 1717/20. Among these are some from the last half of 1719, which we shall nevertheless distinguish from the others, and first of all show in general how, according to the decision of the 10th of January to those of Masulipatnam [Masulipatnam], it was permitted that a certain Eramine grave [uncertain: possibly a local official or merchant] from the Company's behalf there was allowed to have the necessary repairs done to the Company's lodge within Golconda [Golconda] at the amount of 45 rupees [modern equivalent: approximately 45 rupees] 23/32, according to the statement of the Brahmin who has oversight thereof, provided that they would investigate once whether the same person was acting in good faith, since he continually comes forward with this and that carpentry work. The aforementioned overseer has also advised that a certain Brahmin and doctor of the Subah's [Subah: a provincial governor] mother had a sprout dug from the Company's water canal, and he complained about it to the regents but received no hearing, whereupon they have been ordered there to protest against it, or otherwise

text_translated_detailed: From the court we had received word that the Emperor—had summoned the Kilietjechan [uncertain: local title] who was going forward to his presence, and for that purpose had dispatched four of His Majesty's guards toward him. Also that Hydercolichan [uncertain: local title] would again send the Dewan [expanded: chief minister] of the Dechance to govern, would have obtained, while here, owing to the excessive rainfall that had fallen in the month of December, within the Company's Lodge a very great abundance of wild vegetation had grown up. I have spoken to the overseer of the water canal toward the Nallacarienarsoe [uncertain: local place name] and asked why he did not cut down the same and keep the Lodge clean of it, but the same person responded to me that this was no concern of his, and that he should only attend to his canal service, et cetera. But considering that the Company's Lodge (besides the fact that the dwelling of the second [officer] also appears completely dilapidated through the wild vegetation that has grown in it) comes to present itself in a very neglected state to the respectable gentlemen here, I therefore request from Coromandel under date 23 February, Year 1721, that you would be pleased to arrange an order concerning this matter and send it to me. In accordance with your esteemed command, I have looked about here to obtain some Labus besour [uncertain: type of goods] for purchase, but I could not procure any from anyone. However, in due course, should some become available, it shall be conveyed to you. Meanwhile, one of the two peons [expanded: messengers/servants] who departed from there with me toward here having become ill, the other departs, accompanied by a [uncertain: text damaged] from here, and returns again toward you. I remain at your service in the future—should any noteworthy news arrive here, the same shall be dutifully communicated to you. We all servants of the general Dutch East India Company, subject under the obedience and command of the same Company, none excepted, promise and swear that we the illustrious high and mighty lords States-General of the free united Netherlands, as our highest and sovereign authority, and the directors of the general Dutch East India Company, likewise also the present Governor-General over East India Henrik Zwaarde Croon shall be faithful and loyal, and that we all orders, both by article letter and ordinances by the aforesaid directors, or also by the well-mentioned Governor-General and Council of India, already made, as those by them and all other our commanders and officers during our service shall yet be made, according to our utmost ability shall fulfill and further follow, in all respects the orders of the aforementioned Governor-General and his council, together with those of our superiors and lesser officers, and thus to do all that in particular by the article letter concerning the servants and by the successive ordinance is expressed. So truly help us God Almighty. Undersigned was signed R. v. Doornik, A. V. Berlekom, G. Westrenen and Son, J. V. After this, his Excellency had the captain of the Haringtuin called and ordered him to make ready to take on the packs lying here prepared. Upon this, that man declared that his decks, since departing from the Cape of Good Hope, had not been properly caulked and leaked in many places, and for that reason he was not in a position to load packs until the decks were properly caulked. When his Excellency asked him again how many caulkers were needed, he answered ten, which his Excellency ordered us to send on board at once, which was done. Moreover, to keep the work progressing as much as possible, the carpenters of the Magdalena were also pressed into service, so that as soon as that work is completed, 251 from Coromandel dated May 3rd

Nagapatnam. To the esteemed and honored Lord Gerrit Westrenen, Governor and Director of this Coromandel Coast with its jurisdiction and the Council. Well-esteemed and honored Lord, and most generous and commanding Lord. This afternoon the ships Magdalena and the Haringtuin have arrived here at this roadstead from Sadraspatnam, under the command of the Lord and Mr. Dirk van Cloon, which vessels, as soon as it shall be possible for us, after the unloading of the cloth packages here in the bandel [warehouse], which will amount to approximately 600 bales, we shall have the aforementioned vessel proceed toward the Coast, although to our particular regret, through lack of coolies [laborers], it will take well 6 or 7 days before we shall be able to complete the aforementioned unloading work, which we have deemed it our duty to communicate to your Esteemed Lordship, under

Nagapatnam To as before This morning Your Esteemed Honors, according to duty, having communicated in what danger the Company's precious vessels found themselves at this roadstead through the suddenly arising and broken storm, we shall now again have the honor to inform Your Esteemed Honors that after the dispatch of the aforementioned humble advice, the wind from the North-east, shifting to the North-west, our concern for the feared misfortunes was somewhat thereby diminished, but yet not without uneasiness and fear that the aforementioned vessels, upon a change of wind from another quarter, and especially when the same might again set itself in the North-east, not only in the same, but in much worse danger might come to be, considering that the aforementioned keels had somewhat gone through, and had approached the shore, and in what harmful change no means could be thought to avoid the greatest misfortune, so we have, for their own preservation, as much as it lay in our limited human power

text_translated_detailed: again into a good state here, when the storm from Coromandel under date 3rd May Year 1721, which continues equally fierce until now, shall have passed, whereby etc a, /was signed/ D: v: Cloon, W„m VZijl, Arn„s oosterharen, and M„r Dfeiffer, /in margin/ Portonovo the 30th March Year 1721. Nagapatnam To as before From our humble writing of yesterday Your Esteemed Honors shall have become aware of the storm that arose here, and the reasons which compelled the Company's vessels to abandon this roadstead and seek the sea, so we now cannot pass by the continuation of that, to communicate to Your Esteemed Honors by means of this with respect, that the storm in the previous night diminishing, finally reached calm, and today the aforementioned ships were not heard from, but according to received report from the sent peons, we have understood that the same yesterday after midday would have timely passed the point of Solderon, so that the aforementioned vessels are driven toward the Coast, and before the receipt from Coromandel under date 3rd May Year 1721, there in safety shall have appeared, which to understand we look forward to from Your Esteemed Honors with great longing, this morning we have had this roadstead visited and in answer understood that they have sent four anchors lying off, of which two of these would be from the herring tun, which we intend tomorrow, if possible, to have fished up, when the maguas, which this morning went to the assistance of the hawaldaar [local official] of this place toward Peria Coepang 2½ hours from here, to fish up some cloth bales from the English Company, which there from a wrecked vessel have been stranded, it is also reported to us today that there is a small vessel laden with linen cloths from the aforementioned nation from Condelour that could have been stranded, whereby etc=a, /was signed,

text_translated_detailed: be able to, have again relieved, during which time we have firmly established that the remaining stock of cloth packages that have been lying here in storage can also still be shipped aboard the Magdalena without any delay being caused, should the other otherwise more numerous vessels from Coromandel under the date of 3rd May, Anno 1721, otherwise have to wait elsewhere, we shall allow the voyage to proceed, even without raising the anchors, if the skippers did not declare that they could not do this without them, so that upon the coming of bad weather, standing in their voyage (which God forbid) they might not get into greater danger of losing the Company's vessels, with which Etc., was signed Dirk van Cloon, W[illem] van Zeijll, Arn[old] Oosterharen, M[ichael] Pfeiffer, in margin Portonovo the 2nd April Anno 1721, My Lord van Cloon, so immediately I receive your letter of the current [date] and it serves as answer that the Company's vessels are now sailing a little north of this Lodge in full sail southward, God grant them safe passage, undersigned Your Excellency's obedient servant (was signed) A[rnold] van den Heuvel in margin Tharangambadi [Tranquebar] the 2nd April anno 1721. text_translated_detailed: together with the Esteemed Council, Well Noble and Venerable, most generous and commanding Lord, The enclosed copies of letters, by the steersmen of the ships the Magdalena and the Haringthuijn [Herring Thuja], to the head merchant van Cloon and the aforementioned skippers, and from Tharangambadi [Tranquebar], this morning with the breaking of day, brought here, shall show Your Excellency in what condition the Company's vessels have been, and in what state they now find themselves, as well as their earnest and urgent request to be provided anew with anchors and ropes, but since we are not in a position to be able to assist them therewith, and have also been rendered unable, from Coromandel under the date of 3rd May, Anno 1721, through the loss of their boats, to have the anchors lying here at the roadstead fished up, we are necessitated to beseech Your Excellency in the most humble manner to be so good as to send a Company's Chaloupe [small boat] here with the greatest speed, to the end that with the help of the same aforementioned anchors with all dispatch to have them raised, in order to rescue the aforementioned vessels from their pressing need, so immediately the aforementioned skippers departed with Chaloups [small boats] to their vessels which now lie near Tharangambadi [Tranquebar], with the recommendation to take good care of their ships, and to continue the voyage hither without delay, and since the steersman of the Haringthuijn in his letter gives notice that some packages in his ship's hold have become wet, so our humble supplication is to learn Your Excellency's good pleasure and order, how one should deal therewith, so that we may thereafter conduct ourselves accordingly, with which Etc., (was signed) Dirk n[amed] Cloon, W[illem] V[an] Zijll, arn[old] Oosterharen, and m[ichael] Pfeiffer. in margin From Coromandel under the date 33rd May, Anno 1721, Portonovo the 3rd April Anno 1721. Portonovo, To the Esteemed Lord Dirk

Portonovo, To the Esteemed Lord Dirk van Cloon, Second of this Coromandel government, Esteemed Lord, These few lines are directed solely with the greatest respect to bring to your knowledge that we are not with the ships the Magdalena and the Haringthuijn about a mile north of the Tharangambadi [Tranquebar] roadstead at anchor, with longing for suitable weather and wind, in order to be able to appear before you, but since we now find ourselves in the utmost difficulty, for anchors and ropes, as we have lost three and the Haringthuijn two pieces at the Portonovo roadstead, as will become clearer to you by the accompanying respectful report, our humble request is to you to be pleased to employ all conceivable from Coromandel under the date of 3rd May, Anno 1721, means to work, so that we may be provided with other anchors and ropes, since we shall find ourselves in the utmost difficulty of the weather upon the raising of any bad weather, through this lack, in the meantime we remain awaiting your much esteemed orders, what it behooves us to do in this present circumstance, which shall be promptly followed by those who have commended you to God's protection, after respectful greeting with the deepest respect remain undersigned Your Excellency's obedient and submissive servants, (was signed) mich[ael] n[amed] Markel and I[saac] Hockeling, (in margin) in the ship the Magdalena the 2nd April 1721, in the evening one hour

text_translated_detailed: We give you honor with our letter from Coromandel dated May 3rd, Year 1721, respectfully communicating that the ship Coijlang, which lay here at the roadstead, departed after noon toward Pondicherry [Phare]. We had hoped to be in a position to lift the anchors lying here at the roadstead, but to our regret, the vessel's commander declared that vessel to be unfit for that purpose, for the reason that the bow was too low and the mast too weak to hoist such heavy anchors and bring them aboard. And since we are informed that there are no small boats [Chialoupen] available at the coast, for which reason we took the liberty this morning to humbly request of you, and that such work could be accomplished with heavy tackle [kattemarauws] (of which there are also none here), our respectful request is that you would be pleased to send us four of such large boats, and such equipment as would be necessary for it. The chief merchant of Cloon will remain here in hope of your approval until such mentioned anchors shall be lifted; and then undertake the journey overland toward the coast, when the ships, contrary to our hope and expectation, from Coromandel dated May 3rd, Year 1721, have not yet appeared here, which can make little progress due to the fierce south winds blowing through, with which, etc. — was signed: Dirk van Cloon, W[illem] v[an] Zijll, Arn[old] Oosterharen, and M[ichiel] Pfeijffer. In the margin: Pondicherry [Portonovo], April 3rd, Year 1721. Nagapatnam. As before. text_translated_detailed: — was signed: Dirk van Cloon, W[illem] v[an] Zijll, Arn[old] Oosterharen, and M[ichiel] Pfeijffer. In the margin: Pondicherry [Portonovo], April 3rd, Year 1721. Nagapatnam. As before. Today around midday, the ships Magdalena and Haringtuin came to anchor at this roadstead, and when their captains came ashore, they were handed the letter directed to them by you and sent with the ship Coijlang. They were also earnestly asked whether they could continue the journey to the coast according to the order mentioned by you in it. Both of them testified that such could not be done without the greatest danger at the slightest increase of wind or rough weather, without first having recovered their lost anchors and ropes. To this they declared they would apply their utmost effort. From Coromandel dated May 3rd, Year 1721, this being taken into consideration, we have been advised to ensure the safety of the aforementioned vessels, in hope of your kind approval, to have the aforementioned captains set to work tomorrow lifting the lost anchors, which we wish will be successful, so that those vessels may steer from here to the coast as quickly as possible. The captains have found the boat of the Haringtuin in the sea in their previous journey to the ships, and brought it aboard with the help of a Tanjore [Tegenspertnamsen] small boat [Chialeng], and according to our information, another vessel had run aground south of the Coodeloor River [Coedeloerse revier], and understanding that it was the boat of the Magdalena, we had the governor [hawaldaar] make this known, who also consented to allow it to be retrieved from there. But when we wanted to put this into effect, one of the governor's soldiers appeared, who hindered the progress—

text_translated_detailed: obedient and humble servants, [was signed] Martinus van Heuven and Johan Hendrik Dormieux, [to the side] from Coromandel dated the 3rd of May in the year 1721. Witnessed by me [signed] Mattijs Pfeiffer [Below] Portonovo, the 8th of April, 1721. — [still below] Agrees [signed] Arnoldus Oosterharen. Agrees. William Crielaart, west clerk. Portonovo and the Honorable designated second of this letter, Dirk van Cloon, together with the chief officers there. Good Friends, your Company's two letters of the 30th of March, on the last and first of the current month, have been received here. We send this in reply, and not without distress and great sorrow have we learned of the danger in which the Company's two ships now find themselves before Portonovo. However, we hope that they, through God's goodness and grace, will yet overcome that same danger without any disaster or misfortune, and that the storm has already passed and subsided. From Coromandel dated the 3rd of May in the year 1721, and since the goods mentioned therein, amounting to a quantity of 100 packages in the aforementioned vessels, have already been shipped, you are instructed not to hold those two ships any longer on account of the aforementioned number of unshipped packages, but rather, as soon as it is at all possible, to have them undertake the journey hither, while we shall easily be able to supply that shortage here from our stock to a full cargo, so that we may have more vessels continue the journey from here to Batavia as speedily as possible, with which, etc. [was signed] G. Westrenen, P. v. Burg, G. Maire, H. Jacobs, A. Pla, Albert v. Weede, I. Immens, H. Haak, Frederick Elliot, B. van Duijn, and Christian Poleman the Younger [in margin] Nagapatnam, the 1st of April in the year 1721. — Portonovo. As before. Haak, Frederick Elliot, B. van Duijn, and Christian Poleman the Younger /in margin/ Nagapatnam the 1st of April Anno 1721, — Portonovo To the aforementioned On your letter of the last of March the 2nd of this month from Coromandel dated the 3rd of May Anno 1721, received from here, we have resolved to send our vessel Coijlang from here, with a letter to the commanders of the ships the Magdalena and Haringthuin to seek them out, and upon meeting to hand it over to them, whereby they are ordered that they must proceed with those two ships without any delay hither, etc., just as the boatswain of the aforementioned vessel is charged with, upon meeting the aforementioned vessels, and after his orders have been carried out, then to continue the journey further to Portonovo, and to inform you thereof, just as we not only give you notice of this decision we have taken, by this letter, but also thereby order that the E. van Cloon, together with the commanders of those 2 ships that may have remained there, must transport themselves hither in the best manner possible, if contrary to our hope and expectation those same vessels have not yet returned from the Coast, and if any packages might still be lying there in storage; you, upon the appearance of the aforementioned vessel, shall have those same loaded into ships there, and let his journey from Coromandel dated the 3rd of May Anno 1721 continue hither with them, whereby etc., /was signed/ G. text_translated_detailed: Tegenepatnam, in hope that before the receipt of this our writing at the roadstead of Portonovo they will have arrived, wherefore we come to renew our order given to that end, for a speedy dispatch of the same hither, and therefore also deem it unnecessary that the remaining packages in the Magdalena be unloaded, so that you as quickly as possible can make up the invoice of the unloaded cloth packages in the vessel to be able to send it hither by the land route, but the remaining in the vessel Coijlang shall be loaded into ships, in order from Coromandel dated the 3rd of May Anno 1721 to return hither with them, therefore also, with the fishing up of the anchors, since the skippers have declared there that without them they cannot continue the journey, as much haste must be made as will be at all possible, seeing that the south winds are beginning to blow more and more each day at this place, and thus could cause a very long journey for those ships, which we wish otherwise from the heart, and therefore at the end of this we shall once more reiterate, that you must not hold up the aforementioned vessels for any reason longer, as soon as they have the aforementioned anchors at home, but must dispatch them without the least loss of time from here, — whereby etc., /was signed/ G. To the well-esteemed, strict, and noble Lord Gerrit Westrenen, Governor and Director of the chartered Dutch Company on the Coast of Coromandel, together with the council, residing within the Castle there. Noble, earnest, wise, aforementioned, most discreet Lord and Friends. In this moment your Excellency's honorable missive of this Van Coromandel under date 3rd May Anno 1721 has come into my hands, on the same day. I had already heard some days ago that your Excellency's Company's ships from the anchor ground at Portonovo had come aground with loss of anchors and ropes, which grieved my heart, but now understanding that they have regained the anchor ground so close by here on the Coast, I have become very glad about the same. It is enough as long as it is preserved; the sustained damage the Lord of Heaven can compensate again. For the anchors there are no stocks, and no wood here at this place that is customary for that purpose.

text_translated_detailed: Denmark, Etc., likewise chief over the state of the Royal Danish Company in India, together with the council, residing within the Castle Dansborg. Van Coromandel under date 3rd May Anno 1722. Noble, earnest, wise, aforementioned, most discreet Lord and Friends. Whereas the Company's ships the Magdalena and Haringtuin, on the 30th of March last, lying at anchor before Portonovo, in that hard storm had the misfortune that they had to abandon that roadstead and seek the sea, in order not to run aground on the shallows and thus come into even greater danger, and by that accident had to leave in the ground there 5 pieces of anchors and five and a half heavy ropes, and also lose two boats and a small boat, with three men, through which damages and losses the ship's officers, who with the aforementioned vessels on the 2nd of this [month], a mile away opposite Patnam, were again driven up, have fallen into great perplexity, finding themselves entirely unable to continue the journey again from this point, as at the least bad weather, God forbid, they would not be able to save themselves at all, and therefore have also requested us to be assisted here. Van Coromandel under date 3rd May Anno 1721. So it is our entirely obliging and friendly request, whether you from your stores cannot spare two anchors and two anchor ropes, suitable for ships of 130 feet, as these are according to our estimation. The cost of the same we shall pay you with thanks, as we here at present do not have a single anchor or rope that is suitable for that purpose. So yes, or whether also the goodness would please to have, from us a speedy answer thereupon to come, as there is haste in it, wherewith your Excellency in the keeping of God be better, and after cordial greeting remain [signed below].

text_translated_detailed: September, Year 1721. From Coromandel, the 5th. To the Most Esteemed and Honored Lord Henrik Zwaardecroon, Governor-General, together with the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies, Most Esteemed and Honored Lord and Lords, In accordance with the order of the Esteemed Lord Governor Gerrit Westrenen and Councillor at Nagapatnam, contained in their missive dated the 9th of the previous month, August, received here on the 25th thereof, when the ship Blijenburg arrived at this roadstead, the aforementioned vessel is hereby dispatched to your Most Esteemed Lordship, with such cargo, packages of cloth, linens, and leather hides, together with ordinary stonework and Calicut wood, as destined for the aforementioned Nagapatnam, and subsequently also for Porto Novo, Sadras, and here at the Comptoir [trading post], has been received, namely, 1615 packages of various cloths and linens from Coromandel dated the 5th of September, Year 1721: 17 packages of fine bleached Guinean cloth, 136 pieces of common rough [cloth], 153 packages, 695 pieces of common bleached Guinean cloth, 6 pieces of bleached blue [cloth], 208 pieces of brown blue [cloth], 2 pieces of fine bleached Salempuri, 13 pieces of common rough Salempuri, 189 pieces of bleached brown blue [cloth], 72 pieces of rough Parcalle, 21 pieces of bleached [Parcalle], pieces of brown blue [cloth], 26 pieces, 21 pieces of bleached Baftas, 18 pieces of brown blue [Baftas], 4 pieces of Boelangs, 6 pieces of Bramdams, 6 pieces of bleached Chiavoni, 4 pieces of common bleached Moeris, 7 pieces of rough [Moeris], 3 pieces of fine broad bleached Bethilles, 33 pieces of narrow [Bethilles], 10 pieces of rough broad [Bethilles], 6 pieces of narrow [Bethilles], 1 piece of common bleached [cloth], pieces of fine bleached Indian type, of 6 pieces, tighter and finer weave, 8 pieces of Ternatan [cloth], 4 pieces of Outisaal [cloth], pieces of brown blue [cloth]. text_translated_detailed: Our letter of the 3rd of May contains detailed information about this matter. Furthermore, we enclose herewith 5 original accounts of the deceased Hendrik Janszoon, constable at Palliacatta [Pallacat/Pulicat]. Hendrik Janszoon was placed in irons and chained, with business papers in a separate cash box with cash, etc., which were made available for convenience. Finally, from Coromandel on the 6th of September 1721, authorization follows, whereby the estate amounts to ƒ 352. 13. 5, according to the register, and attached thereto a testament, which the guardians of orphans of this city respectfully request may be placed on the roll of authorization, to obtain qualification, so that the said amount may be paid out to the heirs of the deceased here. A criminal sentence: slaves, three of them, own persons, for theft, given by Abram Davitsz and his widow, etc., for theft committed against the goods of their mistress, condemned by the council of justice here on the 20th of May, to be whipped, branded, and further chained in irons, forever slaves of the Company; and to remain so. A separate small cash box with salary books and other papers according to a special register; likewise Coromandel business books and also a claim. text_translated_detailed: Well, the cause has been that my previously written letter slipped from my mind, therefore I waited until after the departure of said ships before I wished to inquire after them. From your Excellency's honorable letter of the 21st of this month, understanding your Excellency's affection with the presentation of the mentioned rope work, which obliges me to your service, always ready to be of use, if your Excellency can provide these sorts, such as ¼ pieces of Dutch cable-rope of 9 inches thick, 6 inches thick, 5. 1. ½. 1. —. please let me know the price of this, and when that is known, I shall send a chialeng [a type of small vessel], to fetch it according to your Excellency's pleasure, whereby I commend your Excellency's generous person to the protection of God, while with cordial greetings and service presentation I remain [undersigned] well-esteemed and honored Lord, your Excellency's service-ready friend and servant [was signed] C. v. van Nissen, [in margin] Castle Dansbourg on the [blank] of May, Year 1721. [Postscript] I am informed by a vessel come from the coast of Malabar that the English place Anjanga shall be abandoned by this nation, and the English killed. From Coromandel under date 6th of September 1721. If that is true, they will suffer great damage here. I would be doing myself a great service if your Excellency could spare one or half a barrel of tar. Nagapatnam As before, since your Excellency's honorable letter of yesterday has arrived, I have already sent out a chialeng to fetch the rope work, but regarding the price I have not been able to receive instruction, what currency your Excellency wishes to understand by the mentioned amount, therefore if it shall be meant in guilders, I request that your Excellency be pleased to send along with the chialeng these three [items/instructions].

From Tranquebar [Tranquebar:] To the well-born, strict, honourable Christian Ulrich van Nissen, Governor of His Royal Majesty of Denmark &c., and likewise chief officer over the state of the Royal Danish Company in India, residing within the Castle Dansbourg, with the Council. Noble, earnest, valiant, wise, aforementioned, very discreet Lord and Friend. With some occupations and indisposition, I have not been able to answer your Honour's writings sooner than this date, whereby now in accordance with the request made, your Honour is informed of the prices of the ropes, as follows: 1 piece of Holland cable rope of 9 inches costs ƒ 306 [guilders]. From Coromandel under date 6 September 1721. 1 piece of Holland cable rope of 6 inches costs ƒ 204. Of 5 inches ƒ 153. Of 7 inches ƒ 250. text_translated_detailed: and since it ran aground close to the shore, all the goods and money were salvaged; but since at that place the Lodge of Your Excellency is located, the servants came immediately and took in such manner the money and the goods, which together amount to 24,000 silver ropias [modern equivalent: Indian rupees], to carry away, and the gentlemen of the Lodge have furthermore, by force, extracted a declaration from the Captain, bookkeeper, and other officers of the ship, as if nothing was found in the ship, whereas there were 200 persons on it, and the majority of them have arrived here at Masulipatsnam, and I swore in the hearing of the Cadi [a Muslim judge], and other qualified persons of the justice, that those of the Lodge had taken all the goods and the money, which was found in the ship, for themselves. I have made many complaints to the former chief of Masulipatsnam, the present (Esteemed and respectable Lord) Governor of Nagapatnam, to whom my petition was never heard. I am the governor of this Masulipatsnam, and I perform all services of the ships and the Company without fail, and since I do so much good for the Company, I also expect from Your Excellency that you will do me equal right, by sending someone, and a letter with express order, to restore to me all the taken money and goods, and I shall remain entirely obliged to you for this, and make Your Excellency highly renowned, in no times is this Coromandel Coast dated the 6th of September 1721. matter happened, I hope that in that of your Excellency's government, it also shall not happen, to incur no bad reputation, [undersigned] agrees [signed] Hermanus Taarling, second and first written clerk, (Lodger) for the translation Masulipatsnam, the 23rd of March, Year 1721. (signed) h.

Extract of letter by the Esteemed Mr. Gerrit Westrenen, chief merchant and chief officer over North Coromandel together with the council at Masulipatnam dated 16th March 1719 to the Esteemed Sir Adriaan de Visser, Governor and Director of this Coromandel Coast, together with the council at Nagapattinam [Nagap=n:]. The great Governor here, Kodaji Ibrahim, having for some months past caused it to be made known to us that a ship named Fatti Moerat belonging to him, and coming from Surat [Souratta:] with his cargo hither, was driven by haste or tempestuous weather on the Ceylon [Cheijlonce:] coast of Coromandel under date 6th September 1721, between Colombo and Point Galle [Punte Galo:], at a place named Bentota, ran aground, and by the Company's servants there, the cargo was to be unloaded from it, and stored in three warehouses, with the desire that restitution of the same should be effected. However, having remained silent regarding this matter for some time, until the 26th January, the same, notwithstanding that we have let him know that this matter does not concern us at all, and that he could send a proxy to Ceylon, has renewed his claim under various threats, and has sent us an inventory of the cargo that was loaded in the aforementioned his wrecked ship, the cost of which amounted to rixdollars [modern equivalent: silver coins] 25098 3/24, sent in Persian, of which the copy and translation hereof is enclosed. And since we are not without fear that he, as Governor, will trouble us further with this matter, and by non-payment bring obstacles concerning the Company's interests, we therefore humbly request that Your Esteemed Excellency deign to write the necessary to the Esteemed Honored Sir, the Governor of Ceylon and council at Colombo, so that we may thus be placed in a position, upon further demonstration by him, the Governor, to defend ourselves against the same with Your Esteemed Excellency's advice and opinion regarding the penalty therein set forth, from Coromandel under date 6th September, Year 1722, on a firm foundation. (noted below) agrees (was signed) Hermanus Taarling, first Clerk. (Below) agrees W. Crielaart, first Clerk. text_translated_detailed: From the Coromandel Coast under date 6th September Anno 1721. Nagapatnam, To the well Noble and esteemed Lord Gerrit Westrenen, Governor and Director of this Coast of Coromandel, with the jurisdiction thereof. Together with the Esteemed Council, Yesterday we had the honor to receive your Lordship's most venerable Letters of the 14th current, whereby you have been pleased to command us to send with the first sea opportunity from our cash reserves 20 to 25,000 pagodas [modern equivalent: Indian gold coins] to the Pondicherry [Pondichierry] chief, and since the Chialoup [small sailing vessel] Eddemonij, which had been dispatched to the Coast on the 16th of this month, had not advanced even half a mile from here due to the strong south winds, we have in dutiful compliance with your Lordship's aforementioned order sent with that small vessel to the said Comptoir [trading post] on the Coromandel Coast under date 6th September 1721, 15,000, that is fifteen thousand pagodas, since upon further consideration we feared that if we had sent 20 to 25,000 pagodas, we ourselves might not have sufficient cash reserves before the onset of the coming impassable monsoon season. Since the last report that the undersigned chief here, dated 27th March of last year, through his respectful and singular letter to your Lordship, made regarding the trade of the Ostenders [Dutch East India Company competitors from Ostend] at Covelong and the condition of that place—these people, through the departure of the Lord Nabab [Indian ruler] Tadoulachan to the north, have returned without any satisfaction having been obtained regarding his complaint to their Esteemed common residence place, but their Esteemed inland protector Marechitti, not being able to tolerate the Moorish regent there, Miab Zeeb, has taken his departure to a small place called Carrenj, which lies halfway between Covelong and Masulipatnam, belonging to a certain Gulamelichan, brother-in-law of the Lord Nabab, from whom protection had been promised to him, having a small house built there, and moved the Coromandel Coast under date 6th September

text_translated_detailed: From Coromandel under date 6th September, Anno 1721, — In the Name of the holy God, Exalted Lord Governor To the high general of the Company, who comes to the aid of the needy, and protects them by her lawful right, and whose feet we humbly kiss, as having the power to govern her subjects in his administration through justice, and to render right to those to whom, matters are His Excellency's utterance in lawfulness require, we request to obtain a sufficient and friendly consideration, to the end that our minds may be brought to a good peace, on account of a certain vessel, which bears the name of fatek Morad, — and having departed from Surat to Masulipatnam, was stranded on the way, according to the news which we have since received from there; being between Colombo and Natuba and Galle, all subordinate places of the Island Ceylon come to be lost, and there through the negligence of the helmsmen struck upon the rocks, and dashed to pieces, such From Coromandel under date 6th September 1721 yet that through God's goodness the goods were salvaged, and brought safely to land, meanwhile nevertheless the Captain of Baldtjiri, and that of Galle, with the fiscal did not hesitate to join in, and to seize all the goods thereof, and have them carried away, having thereupon indeed given a petition for the recovery of those goods to the same, but they nevertheless could not resolve to restore the same to us; having remained under their power, the number of 200 Moslems and 100 heathens, likewise in their Lodge laid the cargo of that ship as well as the value of twenty-four thousand silver ropies [modern equivalent: rupees], in cash, with yet some other necessities of value, although we have not failed since

text_translated_detailed: From Coromandel under date the 15th September Anno 1721. Translation of the letter of the overseer over the Company's Lodge at Golconda named Ammara Singoe to the Esteemed Lord Paulus Verrijn, chief merchant and chief, of northern Coromandel, chartered sub-date the 18th. Current; and on the 23rd thereof here delivered, being of the following content. After compliments &c. text_translated_detailed:
From Coromandel, the 6th of October in the year 1721, Batavia. To the Most Noble and Esteemed Lord Henric Zwaardecroon, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords, Councillors of the Netherlands India.

Most Noble and Esteemed, Commanding Lord, and Esteemed Lords,

On the 24th of September last past, there arrived here in the afternoon at half past four o'clock at the roadstead the ship Voorburg [Voorburg], and that same evening the bookkeeper came ashore, delivering to us the esteemed writings from our respective lords, the governors of Masulipatnam [Masulipatnam], from which it became clear to us that Their Excellencies had sent to this trading post for commerce and such purposes 6,000 pagodas [pagodas: Indian currency] in ready cash, namely 5,000 pagodas in gold and 1,000 in copper coinage. The cargo consists of 69,055¼ pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 31,400 kilograms] of Japanese copper in 550 chests.

From Coromandel, the 6th of October in the year 1721:
12 chests of tapioca flour
3 dozen nutmegs
30 ells [modern equivalent: approximately 56 meters] of scarlet cloth
6 pounds of common penknives
1 Japanese shield
1 cellar of distilled waters
1 barrel of French brandy
1 ream of large and folio format Dutch paper
1 half-ream of small blue writing paper
1 barrel of cardamom
2 bundles of shafts
12 pounds of gall nuts
12 pounds of copperas
12 pounds of gum
1 bundle of Javanese rattan
50 pounds of gunpowder
2 barrels of tar

All of which have been properly delivered by the ship's officers according to regulations, after which we have loaded onto this vessel 350 packages of various cloths, namely 92 packages of common guineas, that is 61 dozen of bleached pieces for the homeland and 31 dozen of raw pieces for the same destination. 112 packages of common bleached Salempuri cloth, namely 63 packages of bleached pieces for the homeland and 49 dozen of raw pieces.

Most Noble and Esteemed, Most Strict and Honored Lords and Gentlemen, Your Excellencies' most obedient, faithful, dutiful, and obedient servants, was signed Ras van Doornik A braham M artinus van Berlekom G errit Westrenen, G errit Westrenen Jr. in margin Bimilipatnam Bimilipatnam, the 6th of October in the year 1721. The above-mentioned letters and further documents have been properly collated by us, the undersigned commissioners, against the content of their respective principals and found to accord therewith. Batavia, in the Castle, the 30th of September, in the year 1722. W illem V an Donk Gallart
